prompt: `They were charged twice for order 4471.` came to ten tokens for seven words. Name one reason given for the difference.
hint: Look at how it was sent.

choices.text: The harness adds the prompt's instructions to the count
choices.why: `tokens.py` sends the text alone, raw, with nothing around it.

choices.text: `tokens.py` counts letters, not words
choices.why: It reads the model's own count; 40 characters is a different number.

choices.text: The line break and the split number
choices.why: Right: punctuation, numbers and the line break all count.

choices.text: Every word in English is two tokens
choices.why: Common words are usually one token each.

prompt: Put inside one JSON field, `{"summary": "…"}`, the ten-token sentence came to how many tokens?
The reply to `t01` is 28 tokens. What are the tokens that are not the summary?

choices.text: The frame: names, labels and punctuation
choices.why: Right: in a JSON answer much of what is written is structure.

choices.text: The prompt's instructions, copied back
choices.why: Those are tokens in, not out.

choices.text: Padding Ollama adds to round the count
choices.why: Nothing is padded.

choices.text: Tokens the model spent thinking before it answered
choices.why: `llama3.2:3b` writes no hidden reasoning here; every token is in the reply.

prompt: Does `tokens.py`'s count tell you what a provider will bill for the same text?

choices.text: Yes, as long as the text is English
choices.why: Language changes the count; it does not make tokenisers agree.

choices.text: No, because providers bill by characters
choices.why: They bill by their own tokens.

choices.text: Yes, because a token is the same unit everywhere
choices.why: Each model splits text its own way.

choices.text: No: each model counts its own way
choices.why: Right: what carries over is the proportion, not the number.

prompt: A cap chosen by thinking about how long the ___ should be comes out too small, because the frame around it is counted too.
With `num_predict=25`, how many of the forty replies passed every check?
Under the cap of 25 there were thirty `json` failures, and `grep -c` counted twenty-nine cut off. What was the thirtieth?

choices.text: A reply cut off at exactly 25 tokens that happened to parse
choices.why: A reply that parses does not fail `json`.

choices.text: `t38`, broken by its apostrophe
choices.why: Right: a different failure with the same check name.

choices.text: A reply the model refused to write
choices.why: Every reply came back.

choices.text: A reply cut off at 24 tokens
choices.why: That is still a cut, and would have been counted.

prompt: A reply ends with `stop: length`. What does that tell you?

choices.text: The model ran out of memory
choices.why: That would be an error, not a stop reason.

choices.text: The model finished on its own
choices.why: That is `stop: stop`.

choices.text: The cap ended it, wherever it had got to
choices.why: Right: the reply is incomplete, whether or not it parses.

choices.text: The reply was too long for the terminal
choices.why: The stop reason comes from the model, not the terminal.

prompt: A colleague sets `num_predict` to 20 on a prompt that writes one-paragraph replies to customers, to keep them short. What happens?

choices.text: Replies arrive cut mid-sentence
choices.why: Right: ask for brevity in the prompt, and keep the cap far above it.

choices.text: The model refuses replies that would be longer than 20 tokens
choices.why: It writes until it is stopped.

choices.text: Nothing, because a cap only applies to JSON
choices.why: A cap applies to any text.

choices.text: The replies come back as shorter paragraphs
choices.why: The model is not told about the cap; it is cut at it.

prompt: Under `v4-words.txt`, `t37` came back shorter and still valid JSON, while the cap of 25 cut replies off mid-string. What is the difference?

choices.text: The request is stricter than the cap
choices.why: The request is weaker: nothing obliges the model to obey it.

choices.text: The cap only applies to the summary
choices.why: It applies to the whole reply.

choices.text: They are the same mechanism with different numbers
choices.why: One is part of the prompt; the other stops generation.

choices.text: The model reads one and not the other
choices.why: Right: asking shapes, the cap only cuts.

prompt: Mean output tokens went from 28.8 to 25.3 when the prompt asked for under 12 words. By how many tokens per reply did the mean fall? Give one decimal.
Asking for a shorter summary also made `t38` parse. Why?

choices.text: The request repaired the JSON after it was written
choices.why: Nothing repairs it; the model wrote a different reply.

choices.text: With fewer words, *won't* never came up
choices.why: Right: the apostrophe that broke the object never came up.

choices.text: The cap stopped the reply before the apostrophe
choices.why: This run had no cap.

choices.text: `v4-words.txt` asks for JSON more firmly
choices.why: Only the summary line changed.

prompt: Under `num_predict=25`, the prompt asking for under 12 words still had nine replies cut. What should change?

choices.text: Remove the request, since the cap does the work
choices.why: The cap cuts; it does not make answers shorter.

choices.text: Ask for even fewer words
choices.why: Any reply over the cap is still cut.

choices.text: Raise the cap above the longest reply
choices.why: Right: the cap guards against a reply that ignores the request.

choices.text: Lower the cap to 20 to be safe
choices.why: A lower cap cuts more.

prompt: Which of these are true of asking for a length in the prompt? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The model reads it and writes a different, shorter answer
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: It moved four categories in this lesson
choices.why: Yes: a line about length is still a line.

choices.text: It guarantees the reply stays under the number given
choices.why: Nothing obliges the model to count correctly.

choices.text: It keeps the JSON closed, where a cap would cut it
choices.why: Yes: the brace is part of what was written.

prompt: Where does choosing a cap start?

choices.text: At the longest ordinary reply you measured
choices.why: Right: 38 tokens over seventy messages.

choices.text: At the length you would like the summary to be
choices.why: That gives a cap that cuts ordinary replies.

choices.text: At the provider's maximum
choices.why: Then the cap guards against nothing.

choices.text: At the mean reply length
choices.why: Half the replies are longer than the mean.

prompt: With the confidence field added and a cap of 76, how many tokens was the longest reply?
Under a cap of 38, seven replies with the confidence field were cut; at 76 all seven passed. What does that show?

choices.text: A higher cap makes the model write better answers
choices.why: The cap does not change what is written, only where it stops.

choices.text: The sign test was wrong
choices.why: Seven fixed and none broken is p = 0.016, a real difference.

choices.text: The confidence field makes the model less accurate
choices.why: The same prompt passed seven more once nothing was cut.

choices.text: The old maximum left no headroom
choices.why: Right: one field moved the maximum from 38 to 43.

prompt: A reader adds the missing closing brace to a reply cut after its last field, parses it, and gets the right answer. Why is that still a bad rule for every cut reply?
hint: Where else can a cut land?

choices.text: Because adding a brace is slow
choices.why: Speed is not the issue.

choices.text: Elsewhere a repair accepts a wrong reply
choices.why: Right: every reply that hit the cap is a failure.

choices.text: Because JSON forbids adding characters
choices.why: JSON has no opinion; the question is what the repair accepts.

choices.text: Because the stop reason would change
choices.why: The stop reason says `length` whatever the reader does.

prompt: Why does `v9-confidence.txt` need the `sed` edit to `pl.py` before its replies can pass?

choices.text: Because Ollama rejects JSON with four fields
choices.why: Ollama does not check the reply.

choices.text: Because `pl.py` cannot read numbers
choices.why: It reads them fine; the issue is the key.

choices.text: `judge()` refuses keys it does not know
choices.why: Right: the check is the reader's needs, and the reader needs one more key.

choices.text: Because the prompt file has a header the harness does not understand
choices.why: This prompt has no header.

prompt: Put the steps of setting a cap in order.
hint: Measure, then set, then measure again.
items: Run the prompt over every case without a cap
Set the cap well above it
Measure again whenever the prompt changes

prompt: Match each command to what it told you in this lesson.

pairs.right: How many tokens a text is
The mean and longest reply of a run
The stop reason of one reply

right_distractors: The price of a run in dollars

prompt: After a prompt change, `pl check` starts reporting `json` failures with the reason `cut off at num_predict`. What do you do first?
hint: What did the change do to the replies?

choices.text: Measure the new longest reply and raise the cap
choices.why: Right: the cap has drifted into ordinary traffic.

choices.text: Lower the temperature
choices.why: Temperature does not decide where the cap falls.

choices.text: Ask for shorter answers in the prompt and keep the cap
choices.why: That may help, and it leaves a cap with no headroom.

choices.text: Repair the cut replies by closing their braces
choices.why: A cut reply is a failure; repair hides what was lost.
